extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and political theory; those studying Plato's Republic and the education/qualities of rulers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and educational program Plato advances for selecting and forming guardians/philosopher-kings: the natural gifts, character tests, staged training, and highest knowledge (the Good) required for true rulers. Emphasis on who counts as a genuine philosopher and how the State should cultivate and use them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher's natural gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: “quickness and memory and courage and magnificence—these were admitted by us to be the true philosopher’s gifts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato treats several innate or early-developing qualities as essential (quick intelligence, memory, sagacity, cleverness, high-spiritedness, magnanimity). He warns these qualities rarely grow together and often occur only in 'shreds and patches'—so selection must look for their conjunction. Candidates lacking a sufficient combination should not be entrusted with the highest education or rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to flattery, ambition and worldly corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers will be objects of flattery and requests for favors from friends and citizens who want future power; they may be tempted to vain pomp and senseless pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true philosopher must resist social pressures that divert him from study into politics or personal aggrandizement. The text gives the scenario of a celebrated youth being flattered into ambition and stresses that only one who will 'get understanding' by 'slaving for it'—not being swayed by honors—can become a philosopher. Anti-pattern: a philosopher who yields to praise and uses philosophy for social advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staged, age-appropriate education (body then soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: “In childhood and youth their study, and what philosophy they learn, should be suited to their tender years: during this period ... the chief and special care should be given to their bodies ... as life advances and the intellect begins to mature, let them increase the gymnastics of the soul; but when the strength of our citizens fails ... then let them range at will.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training is explicitly staged: early emphasis on physical training (gymnastics), later increasing intellectual training, and in old age freedom from serious labour. The education must be continuous and progressive rather than a brief youthful dabbling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to the longer, dialectical route to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates must be 'required to take the longer circuit, and toil at learning as well as at gymnastics' and not be content with a 'popular exposition' of justice and virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guardian must pursue deep dialectic rather than stopping at superficial accounts. Socrates criticizes those who abandon dialectic when faced with its difficulty; the ideal guardian endures the rigorous, protracted intellectual work required to reach highest truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the Good (highest knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one who knows 'the idea of good'—the cause of truth and of science—can be a true guardian; knowledge of the good is the supreme principle needed to order the State rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Good is analogized to the sun (author of visibility and growth): it both enables knowing and gives being/essence. Without knowledge of the Good all other knowledge or possessions profit nothing; thus selection and education prioritize the capacity to grasp this highest form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of truth; disinterest in mere appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: The true philosopher 'has surely no time to look down upon the affairs of earth' and is 'a lover of truth and being' rather than concerned with 'persons' or appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians must be motivated by genuine pursuit of truth, not by reputation, contention, malice, or envy. The philosopher imitates the fixed and immutable order and therefore will not engage in vituperative politics or sophistical personal attacks—anti-patterns of the pretender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tested patriotism: fidelity under pleasures, pains, dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers are to be 'lovers of their country, tried by the test of pleasures and pains, and neither in hardships, nor in dangers, nor at any other critical moment [to] lose their patriotism—he was to be rejected who failed, but he who always came forth pure, like gold tried in the refiner’s fire, was to be made a ruler.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character testing by exposing candidates to trials is required; only those who remain steadfast are approved. This is both a moral filter and a selection mechanism for reliable guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of opposing temperaments (quickness + steadfastness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both quick intelligence and a steadfast, dependable temperament are necessary; yet these qualities are rarely united—those quick and spirited are often disorderly, while the steady tend to torpor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection must find candidates who uniquely combine intellectual vivacity with disciplined steadiness. This tension explains the rarity of suitable guardians and the need for careful probations to determine whether a soul can sustain the highest tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of learning and endurance for highest study
rubrics_metrics.description: The aspirant 'must be exercised also in many kinds of knowledge, to see whether the soul will be able to endure the highest of all, or will faint under them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before exposure to the supreme science (the Good), candidates should be schooled across many disciplines to test intellectual stamina and adaptability. This breadth both screens for capacity and conditions the mind for dialectic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to grasp and move between visible (opinion) and intelligible (knowledge) realms
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates draws the likeness of the sun and the 'divided line' dividing visible (images, animals, becoming) and intelligible (hypotheses, principles, ideas); the guardian must understand these distinctions and how knowledge relates to truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes moving from images and opinions up to principles (and ultimately to the Good). Practical implication: guardians should not legislate from mere appearances; they must reason from the intelligible forms to shape institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repudiation of pretenders and sophistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Many unworthy persons enter philosophy attracted by 'fair names and showy titles' and produce 'sophisms captivating to the ear, having nothing in them genuine'; they are likened to a 'bald little tinker' newly in fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit anti-pattern: avoid those who pursue philosophy for status, who substitute rhetoric for true insight, or who make persons rather than things the theme of conversation. The State must distinguish genuine philosophers from imitators and keep the latter from corrupting the discipline and public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to rule when necessary without corrupting aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Either philosophers must be 'compelled...to take care of the State' or rulers (kings/sons of kings) must be 'divinely inspired with a true love of true philosophy'—and if one such philosopher rules he can create the ideal polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers must be prepared to govern when circumstance demands, but their rule should be motivated by knowledge of the Good and the public benefit rather than personal power. The text allows for compulsion or divine-like inclination as mechanisms to place philosophers in power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay lawmaking until the State is prepared by a proper 'clean surface' and model
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators 'will have nothing to do either with individual or State, and will inscribe no laws, until they have either found, or themselves made, a clean surface' and will 'take the State and the manners of men, from which, as from a tablet, they will rub out the picture, and leave a clean surface.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guideline for constitutional design: reforms and laws should be based on a clear account of ideals (the forms) and after removing corrupting influences. This prescribes a preparatory, formative process before concrete legislation is inscribed.
